items.streamTitle: Germany is turning hybrid-threat attribution into a broader defensive architecture
items.streamSummary: Germany is planning a wider anti-sabotage package combining mobile counter-drone units, stronger authorities for critical-infrastructure operators, a national cyber sensor network, and expanded AI-supported surveillance. The development is notable because the response is becoming a sociotechnical defense system rather than a statement of condemnation. It is still a plan, however: implementation quality, public reassurance, adversary behavior, legal sufficiency, and privacy consequences remain separate outcomes that cannot be inferred from the announcement.

items.streamTitle: Influence can begin as a job, trip, or opportunity—not an argument
items.streamSummary: Taiwan’s Straits Exchange Foundation warned that youth-facing job offers, tourism, and cultural exchanges involving China can combine economic opportunity with scam, detention, data, and political-influence risks. The useful analytical point is the pathway: an initial behavioral ask can look ordinary long before any ideological or political objective becomes visible. The warning comes from a Taiwan institution engaged in cross-strait competition, so legitimate exchanges, criminal scams, political influence, and state direction should remain separate evidentiary questions.
items.attribution: Chen Yu-fu & Jonathan Chin — Taipei Times

items.streamTitle: A digital twin needs a continuing connection to the real world
items.streamSummary: A new architecture paper draws a useful boundary between a crowd simulation and a crowd digital twin. A true twin requires sensing and synchronization with the physical crowd and its environment, alongside prediction and decision support; representational detail alone is not enough. The framework is a roadmap rather than evidence that a fully validated crowd twin already exists, but it provides a stricter standard for claims about synthetic audiences and digital twins.
items.attribution: Casadei et al. — Future Generation Computer Systems

items.streamTitle: Synthetic populations are starting to include values and ideology—not just demographics
items.streamSummary: A Bayesian population-synthesis framework adds values, ideology, opinions, and life priorities to the demographic attributes normally used to construct synthetic populations. In a Barcelona demonstration, the method reproduced important demographic and motivational distributions and dependencies across large samples. This creates a more empirical starting point for agent models than demographic personas alone, but it does not show that the resulting synthetic people will make human-like decisions or respond correctly to interventions.

items.streamTitle: Exposure to untrustworthy sources fell about 70%; measured political attitudes did not
items.streamSummary: A multimonth randomized Meta field experiment reduced Facebook and Instagram feed exposure to repeatedly untrustworthy sources by about 70%. Despite that large change in what people saw, researchers found no measurable effects across numerous preregistered political attitudes and beliefs, including among users with high prior exposure. The result does not show that misinformation never matters. It shows why exposure is an intermediate outcome: a technically successful feed intervention can still produce a null at the attitude level.

items.streamTitle: Let an FCM learn without letting it silently invent the graph
items.streamSummary: A human-centric Fuzzy Cognitive Map framework separates reasoning over a fixed graph from a learning loop that updates weights and from explicit bounded expert correction. That architecture allows adaptation while preserving inspectable structure and a record of human intervention. It offers a useful governance pattern for decision support, but the medical benchmarks do not establish that learned edges are causal or that the method transfers unchanged to behavioral or national-security systems.

items.streamTitle: Ordinary citizens persuaded political opponents surprisingly often—but could not tell when they were good at it
items.streamSummary: An incentivized persuasion study asked ordinary citizens to write messages for people who disagreed with them politically. Nearly 30% of the messages shifted opinion in the intended direction and about 11% backfired. Perspective-taking and personal narratives were the strongest predictors of success, yet senders were poor judges of their own persuasive ability. The study shows meaningful message-level heterogeneity, but those features were not independently randomized, so they should not yet be treated as proven causal ingredients.
items.attribution: Naunov, Rueda-Cañón & Ryan — The Journal of Politics

items.streamTitle: AI labels can change how people engage with the same content
items.streamSummary: Two randomized experiments found that labeling social-media content as AI-generated reduced affective and intended behavioral engagement, especially for emotional posts. Disclosure timing also mattered for some AI-enhanced content. The finding suggests that provenance labels can change the experience of a message rather than simply describe it. Because the evidence comes from immediate experimental responses, it does not establish durable changes in trust or observed behavior across an entire platform.

items.streamTitle: Better information reduced party-cue influence; simply thinking harder did not
items.streamSummary: Two large experiments separated access to policy information from prompts to think more effortfully. Providing substantive information reduced reliance on party cues by roughly 35% on average, while encouraging additional thought alone produced little independent effect. The result suggests that some apparent heuristic reasoning reflects an information constraint rather than simple unwillingness to deliberate. The outcomes were policy opinions, not durable political behavior, and effects varied across issues.

items.streamTitle: A government nudge changed when civil servants complied more than whether they complied
items.streamSummary: A Buenos Aires field experiment redesigned the notice attached to real freedom-of-information requests using clarity, salience, deterrence, and social-norm cues. Overall compliance did not significantly increase, but responses exactly at the final legal deadline rose by 10.7 percentage points. Government training workshops diluted the treatment contrast and the researchers also found intra-agency spillovers. The study shows how a treatment can shift the timing distribution while concurrent institutional activity becomes part of the causal story.

items.streamTitle: Causal discovery can help explain an LLM simulation before it explains society
items.streamSummary: CAMO is a new framework for tracing macro-level outcomes in LLM-agent simulations back to smaller sets of simulated mechanisms. It extracts factors from simulation records, learns compact explanatory graphs, and uses simulator-internal counterfactuals to probe ambiguous relationships. That is useful for auditing complex agent systems and identifying model-internal levers. The critical boundary is external validity: a causal pathway recovered inside a simulator is evidence about how that simulator works, not proof that humans follow the same pathway.
items.attribution: Yu et al. — Findings of ACL 2026

items.streamTitle: Pacific leaders’ missile-test response shows why reassurance is part of strategic signaling
items.streamSummary: Pacific Islands Forum leaders expressed concern over China’s ICBM test and called for greater transparency and at least 24 hours’ advance notification, while Nauru dissented and Beijing rejected the criticism. The episode shows that a military demonstration communicates more than capability: warning, consultation, predictability, and perceived respect shape how regional audiences interpret it. Public concern is observable, but the episode does not yet establish a durable change in alignment, deterrence, or security behavior.

items.streamTitle: Movement and environmental feedback can reverse cooperation dynamics
items.streamSummary: A mathematical public-goods model shows how spatial movement can reverse seemingly intuitive cooperation dynamics. Under some conditions, diffusion increased cooperation and public-good availability, while strong movement of cooperators toward resource-rich areas reduced both cooperation and environmental quality. The result is theoretical rather than a human behavioral estimate, but it illustrates an important systems lesson: changing where people cluster, connect, or move can alter the incentives and feedback that determine collective outcomes.
items.attribution: Zhao et al. — Bulletin of Mathematical Biology

items.streamTitle: Rich LLM digital twins still predicted individual human behavior weakly
items.streamSummary: A Science Advances mega-study built individualized LLM digital twins from more than 500 prior answers per person and tested them across 19 preregistered studies, 164 outcomes, and 1,784 participants. Average twin–human prediction correlations were only about .20, with systematic problems including stereotyping, ideological bias, hyper-rationality, and overly compressed responses. The study tests current approaches rather than placing a ceiling on future systems, but it is strong evidence that rich personal context and fluent personas do not automatically produce reliable individual behavioral prediction.

items.streamTitle: Saying “you” can trigger reactance and persuade less than saying “I”
items.streamSummary: Across seven experiments, recommendations framed as “you’ll like this” were often less persuasive than first-person statements such as “I like this.” Second-person wording increased psychological reactance, particularly among people already prone to reactance and when the recommender had little reason to know the audience’s preferences. The effect largely disappeared for close friends. The finding suggests that personalization without legitimate audience knowledge can feel controlling rather than relevant, although most outcomes were evaluations or intentions rather than durable real-world behavior.

items.streamTitle: Norms tighten when observers are present—and more when they have higher status
items.streamSummary: A cross-cultural study of 25,384 adults in 90 societies found that everyday behaviors were judged more constrained when other people were present and more constrained still when observers held higher status. The pattern suggests that norms are not simply fixed rules attached to a behavior or culture; audience presence and hierarchy change the social constraint around the same act. The outcomes were appropriateness judgments rather than observed behavior, so the study is strongest as evidence about normative perception.
items.attribution: Simpson et al. — American Sociological Review

items.streamTitle: AI assistance increased real property-tax appeal filing—but benefits were unequal
items.streamSummary: A preregistered field experiment with 645 Dallas County households found that adding an AI chatbot to an otherwise similar personalized tax-appeal website increased self-filed appeals from 41.4% to 50.5%. Most households with access used the assistant, and process data suggest it helped people work through available information. The effect was smaller among less-advantaged households, showing that equal access to an AI tool does not guarantee equal behavioral benefit. The study is an NBER working paper and the longer-run financial outcomes remain separate questions.
items.attribution: Holz et al. — NBER Working Paper

items.streamTitle: An intervention can keep propagating through social networks after researchers leave
items.streamSummary: A field experiment in 16 Ugandan villages randomly assigned about 40% of households to a perspective-taking conversation about refugees. Treated participants showed warmer attitudes immediately, but the influence process did not stop there: two to three weeks later, untreated people with more treated network neighbors also tended to hold warmer views, especially through strong ties. The endpoint was attitude rather than observed behavior, but the study provides unusually useful evidence that interpersonal spillovers can continue after formal exposure ends.

items.streamTitle: Propaganda was more persuasive when appeals matched stable psychological needs
items.streamSummary: A multi-method study in China found that propaganda appeals tied to belonging, self-esteem, or value expression produced larger pro-regime attitude shifts among people whose corresponding psychological need was stronger. A follow-up that primed the need without matching the content did not produce the same pattern, supporting a message–audience fit interpretation rather than simple activation. The results strengthen the case for heterogeneous persuasion effects, though the outcomes were mainly attitudes and the political context limits simple generalization.

items.streamTitle: A social-media virtual twin needs networks, recommenders, and feedback loops—not just personas
items.streamSummary: YSocial is a modular LLM-powered virtual social-media environment in which agents can post, comment, react, follow, receive recommendations, and reshape their network over time. A demonstration used two 500-agent partisan populations across 60 simulated days, making exposure and topology part of the model rather than treating each persona as an isolated respondent. The architecture is useful for studying platform feedback, but the authors appropriately describe it as a virtual rather than validated digital twin because real-world behavioral calibration remains limited.
items.attribution: Rossetti et al. — Big Data & Society

items.streamTitle: Participatory FCMs can expose local leverage assumptions without pretending they are causal estimates
items.streamSummary: A participatory Fuzzy Cognitive Mapping study in Oaxaca combined ten local facilitators’ mental models into a 27-component, 43-edge consensus map and used it to compare shallow and deeper leverage points for agroecological adoption. The value is methodological: local knowledge defines an inspectable hypothesis space, while scenario analysis makes it decision-relevant. The authors explicitly caution that the edge weights are subjective judgments and the simulated leverage points are hypotheses, not experimentally identified causal effects.
items.attribution: Garcia et al. — People and Nature

items.streamTitle: Seeing fewer competitors can make people compete more
items.streamSummary: An incentivized experiment found that aggregate information about peers’ competition choices could produce counter-conformity rather than imitation. When participants saw that relatively few peers had entered a tournament, they became more likely to enter themselves, consistent with interpreting low participation as a strategic opportunity rather than a norm to follow. The study uses a selected sample of competitive MBA students, so the exact effect should not be generalized broadly, but it shows why “social information” does not imply one universal mechanism.

items.streamTitle: German grid incidents show why the hybrid-threat narrative should not outrun attribution evidence
items.streamSummary: German authorities investigated suspected electricity-grid sabotage while a handwritten letter claimed responsibility, but officials had not established that the writer caused the incidents or publicly tied the cases to Russia. The story unfolded amid heightened concern about hybrid threats and a nearby election. That makes the case analytically useful: physical disruption, attribution confidence, elite framing, public threat perception, and electoral effects are separate questions. A broader security narrative should not be used as proof of who conducted a specific incident.

items.streamTitle: Collective victimization does not mechanically produce revenge
items.streamSummary: A Nature Reviews Psychology synthesis argues that collective victimization can lead to very different outcomes because groups differ in how they interpret harm, assess control and resources, and cope with it. The framework separates the victimization event from beliefs, appraisal, perceived agency, coping strategy, and later behavior. Its value is conceptual rather than a single new causal estimate: grievance should not be treated as a fixed-sign predictor of hostility when solidarity, meaning-making, or constructive action are also possible.
items.attribution: Vollhardt et al. — Nature Reviews Psychology
